The Prophet said no one had favoured him more than Abu Bakr, who would be his Khalil if he took one, and ordered every mosque door closed except his.
Abu Bakr built a mosque in his courtyard, praying and weeping as he recited the Quran, which drew pagan women and children and alarmed the Quraysh chiefs.
Dying, Abu Bakr asked Aisha about the Prophet's shroud and the day he died, hoped to die that Monday, and asked to be shrouded in his worn garment.
Abu Bakr pays Jabir the Bahrain money the Prophet had promised; in Mecca he returns Ibn Ad-Daghna's protection, content with Allah's, and waits to emigrate with the Prophet.
Abu Bakr has a Quraishi's shepherd milk a sheep, cools the milk by pouring water over its covered pot, and the Prophet drinks till Abu Bakr is pleased.
When Bahrain's wealth arrives after the Prophet's death, Abu Bakr honours his promises, giving Jabir handfuls of money, and answers his charge of miserliness.
In his illness the Prophet insists Abu Bakr lead the prayer despite Aisha's plea that he is soft-hearted, likening her to Joseph's female companions, and Abu Bakr leads.
Abu Bakr grasped the Prophet was the slave given a choice; the Prophet would have taken him as Khalil, kept only his gate open, and sent a woman to him.
The Prophet defended Abu Bakr, loved him most of men, dreamt of him drawing water, cleared his slack robe of pride, and hoped all Paradise's gates would call him.
Umar denies the Prophet's death until Abu Bakr recites verses on it; at Bani Saida the people pledge allegiance to Abu Bakr, and Aisha says both speeches benefited them.
Ali names Abu Bakr then Umar as best after the Prophet; Abu Bakr scolds Aisha when her lost necklace halts the people, and the Tayammum verse is revealed.
Asked the worst thing the pagans did to the Prophet, Abdullah bin Amr recalls Uqba throttling him at prayer until Abu Bakr pulled Uqba away.
The Prophet tells of a slave choosing what is with Allah over this world; Abu Bakr weeps, is praised for his companionship and wealth, and only his door stays open.
After the Prophet's death Abu Bakr invites anyone the Prophet owed or promised, and, after delays, gives Jabir the Bahrain money promised him, calling miserliness the worst disease.
After Abu Bakr and Umar quarrelled the Prophet grew angry, asking if they would leave him his companion, who said he spoke the truth when others called him a liar.
In the cave Abu Bakr feared the pagans would see them, and the Prophet asked what he thought of two whose third is Allah.
Abu Bakr rebuked Aisha and struck her for holding up the people over her necklace while the Prophet slept on her thigh, and the verse of tayammum was then revealed.
In his fatal illness the Prophet insisted Abu Bakr lead the prayer despite Aisha and Hafsa urging Umar, likening them to the companions of Joseph.
Asked by a woman what to do if she did not find him, the Prophet told her to go to Abu Bakr.
